opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Helen. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'm not much of a talker, but I'll do my best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for some things. We use it for summaries and weather notes. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's about right for me. A tool that helps, with a person still making the calls on the grid. That's how it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Do my shifts, keep up with the drills, help the newest operator settle in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That version sits fine with me.

S0.say: It's useful for some things, like summaries and weather notes.
S0.think: That's how it should be. A tool that helps, with a person making the calls on the grid.
S0.do: Works her shifts, keeps up with drills and helps the newest operator settle in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is the responsible way, especially for something like the power grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some tasks going is fine, if it's the dull ones. What bothers me is fewer beginners. Control room skills take years. If we don't train people now, who takes over from me?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speak up in team meetings about keeping the trainee places. Learn the new tools properly so I can tell when they're wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A small worry about who comes after us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn them so you can tell when they're wrong. Do you expect them to be wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. Software's fine on a normal day. The grid doesn't fail on a normal day.

S1.say: Slow is the responsible way, especially for the power grid.
S1.think: Control room skills take years. If we hire fewer beginners, who takes over from me?
S1.do: Speaks up for keeping trainee places, and learns the new tools well enough to spot when they're wrong.
S1.feel: Mostly fine, a small worry about who comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say essential services need public oversight. You don't let a company's software run the grid just to save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Billing and the office side would get hit first. But once a company sees an agent doing office work, it looks at the control room next. Dispatch decisions are where I'd draw the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back the union's push for rules on automation in essential services. Ask management, in writing, what the plan is for dispatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The line I care about is getting closer.

S2.say: Essential services need public oversight. You don't let software run the grid just to save money.
S2.think: Once they see agents doing office work, they'll look at the control room. Dispatch is where I'd draw the line.
S2.do: Backs the union's push for rules on automation in essential services, and asks management in writing about plans for dispatch.
S2.feel: Uneasy. The line she cares about is getting closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should go back to the public, and essential services shouldn't be handed to whoever builds the best AI. I'd sign petitions on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI matches skilled people at thinking work, it can probably run dispatch on most days. I don't think it's safe on the bad days, but I'm not sure the people deciding would listen to me. And we have two teenagers and a smaller cushion than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Write down every time the software gets something wrong, so there's a record. Cut back at home and build up savings. Look at whether my skills fit a job with the regulator or in safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it'd be on my mind every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it isn't safe on the bad days. Is that the sense of duty talking, or worry about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'd like to think it's mostly duty. I'd be lying if I said the job didn't come into it.

S3.say: The gains should go back to the public. Essential services shouldn't go to whoever builds the best AI.
S3.think: It could run dispatch on most days, but not safely on the bad ones. And I'm not sure anyone would listen to me.
S3.do: Keeps a written record of software mistakes, builds up savings and looks at jobs with the regulator or in safety.
S3.feel: Anxious. On her mind every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before. Essential services need people, and public oversight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots don't add much for me. My work is at a screen. The line crews might change, which makes a storm night harder to picture. But my worry is the same as in the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan. Keep the record, keep saving, keep an eye on regulator jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About the same. Anxious, but steady with it.

S4.say: Essential services need people, and public oversight.
S4.think: Robots don't add much for me. My worry is the same as before.
S4.do: Sticks to the same plan: keeps the record, keeps saving and watches for regulator jobs.
